newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Mobutu says he's fine but Zaire has worries.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu says he's fine but Zaire has worries.

text.p: Zaire's veteran president Mobutu Sese Seko says he is fine after surgery in Europe but news of his illness has raised fears about what will happen after Mobuto dies.
Some commentators said without Mobutu, this Central Africa patchwork country of different ethnic groups would become another Somalia or Liberia, where rival warlords hold sway.
Others say that even if Mobutu recovers, the issue of his health -- unofficially he had prostate surgery -- is now firmly on the agenda ahead of long-delayed elections in May.
"Zaire is a powderkeg," Le Palmares, a daily newspaper close to the opposition, said in an editorial last week.
"If the international community was shocked by the horror of what happened in Rwanda after the death of (president Juvenal) Habyarimana, in Zaire the slaughter threatens to be worse."
Other newspapers, both opposition and pro-Mobutu, expressed similar concerns as the question of a Zaire without Mobutu reared its head.
"Recognised by everyone as head of state, the Field Marshall (Mobutu) is the fuse of national unity," Le Palmares said, suggesting he was a necessary evil in turbulent times.
Mobutu, 66 on October 14, seized power in 1965 in Africa's sprawling equatorial heart, celebrated by British author Joseph Conrad in his novel Heart of Darkness.

Mobutu ruled virtually unchallenged in the chaotic, corruption-plagued nation, where Belgian King Leopold carved out a personal colonial empire in the 19th century with the help of explorer Henry Morton Stanley.

In 1990, opposition protests and pressure from Zaire's foreign partners forced him to start democratic reform, although Zaire's sometime turbulent transition has lagged well behind that of other states in the region.

Mobutu originally called for elections in 1995. But the transitional parliament, an unwieldly grouping of the various branches of Zaire's fractious political family with Mobutu supporters in the majority, agreed to extend the transition by a further two years.

Officially, the reasons were lack of time to organise and the presence of over a million Rwandan Hutu refugees who flooded the east of the country following the 1994 assassination of Habyarimana and massacres by Hutu hardliners of hundreds of thousands of minority Tutsis and moderate Hutus in Rwanda.
Mobutu's illness has added a new dimension to the debate.
"Panic and emotion, worry and despair invaded all circles, both political and military," Le Potentiel, another newspaper close to the opposition reported.

The pro-government Standard said before reports of surgery were confirmed that a Mobutu illness could cause real problems. "If he recovers, his state of health will be skillfully exploited during the election campaign," it said.

Speaking by telephone from Lausanne, Mobutu told state television on Friday that he was fine following surgery in August. "I have been operated on. I am resting. I am not under medical supervision. I am at the hotel," he said.
He said he would return to Zaire "soon" but gave no date.

Mobutu, "elected" unopposed in 1970 and 1984, will contest a presidential election next year for the first time. According to the transitional constitution, multi-party presidential and parliamentary elections must be held by July 1997.
Until then, Zaire has a delicate constitutional problem.
If Mobutu dies, the 1992 transitional constitution states the president of the transitional parliament should take over.
Since parliament sacked Archbishop Laurent Monsengwo last year, it has no president. Two vice-presidents -- one a Mobutu loyalist, one from the opposition -- run the assembly.

The Standard said the death of Mobutu before elections would sow confusion in Zaire. "All the ingredients are there for Zaire to become another Somalia or Liberia with warlords reigning in their home regions," it said.

As if in recognition of the ethnic dimension, parliamentary sources say a new constitution to be put to the vote in a referendum in February envisages a federal Zaire -- a concept previously opposed by Mobutu loyalists.
But with the killings in Rwanda and Burundi continuing, the spectre of Zaire without Mobutu has people worried.

"The post-Mobutu (period) is a black hole which inspires fear," Palmares said. "If the U.N. Secretary-General wants to talk about preventive diplomacy, now is the time to look at our country, considering Zaire as a people in danger."
